case_title: Ganga Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: the defence alleged a quarrel between the accused and the victim's husband; the court rejected this defence. No other relationship stated.
evidence_type: Victim testimony; prior statement to mother-in-law; FIR; medical examination; forensic (FSL) report of semen and spermatozoa on petticoat; seizure evidence
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of s.376 IPC on the finding that the intercourse was with the victim's consent
high_court_outcome: State's appeal allowed; acquittal set aside; convicted under s.376 IPC and sentenced to seven years rigorous imprisonment
neutral_facts: The prosecution case is that the accused approached the victim, a married woman, in an agricultural field at about 6.30 p.m. on 21 December 1987 when she had gone there to relieve herself. The victim alleged that the accused caught hold of her, pushed her to the ground, covered her mouth with one hand, restrained her hands with the other, lifted her petticoat and committed rape on her. She returned home and told her mother-in-law about the incident the same evening. The next day, when her husband returned home, she lodged a complaint at the police station, which was registered as an FIR on 22 December 1987. A doctor who examined her the same evening stated that, as the victim was a married woman habitual to intercourse, no definite opinion could be given on whether she had been subjected to sexual intercourse. No injury was found on her person; the victim explained that she had fallen on her back in a field with a smooth surface where wheat and mustard crops grew. The petticoat and vaginal smear slides were preserved and sent for forensic examination. Police visited the scene on 23 December 1987, seized a blouse, a dhoti and broken bangles, and prepared a site map. The forensic laboratory report recorded spots of semen and spermatozoa on the petticoat. The accused denied having had sexual intercourse with the victim and suggested he had been falsely implicated because of a quarrel with her husband. The victim's mother-in-law denied that suggestion. The victim was not questioned in cross-examination about the seizure of the articles from the field.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years rigorous imprisonment (as stated in the judgment); maximum not stated
physical_harm: No injury found on medical examination the next day; the victim explained she fell on her back in a field
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the prosecutrix (PW-5); corroboration by mother-in-law PW-2; FIR lodged with PW-10; FSL report confirming semen and spermatozoa on petticoat
witness_credibility: Court found PW-5 reliable as a victim-witness, not an accomplice; medical absence of injury explained; omission about seizure not put to her in cross-examination so no ground to doubt; PW-2 denied the enmity suggestion
post_offence_conduct: Not stated (the State submitted the accused absconded and was arrested after ten days; the court recorded no finding on this)
trial_duration: offence: 21.12.1987; trial judgment: 30.11.1988; High Court: 26.06.2003; Supreme Court: 04.07.2013
legal_representation: Appellant: Ravi Prakash Mehrotra (Amicus Curiae) with Vibhu Tiwari. State: Siddhartha Dave, Jemtiben Ao, Vibha Datta Makhija
investigation_status: FIR registered on 22.12.1987; medical examination; scene visited 23.12.1987 and articles seized; charge-sheet filed; trial completed in the Sessions Court
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted. High Court: acquittal set aside and conviction under s.376 IPC with seven years RI. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld
prosecution_argument: Victim's testimony is corroborated by PW-2 and the FIR; the victim is not an accomplice so corroboration is unnecessary; consent is not voluntary participation; the accused absconded and was arrested after ten days
defence_argument: Victim is not a sterling witness; no injuries on medical examination; omission about seizure of articles; FIR scribed by a non-investigating officer; shoddy investigation; false implication due to enmity with victim's husband
legal_principle_applied: Prosecutrix is a competent witness under s.118 Evidence Act and her evidence needs no corroboration as an accomplice's would; prior statements admissible under s.157 for corroboration; defective investigation is not a ground for acquittal unless it casts reasonable doubt
precedent_relied_upon: State of Maharashtra v. Chandraprakash Kewalchand Jain (1990) 1 SCC 550 (relied on); Browne v. Dunn (1894) 6 R 67 (referred to); Narender Kumar (2012) 7 SCC 171, Rai Sandeep (2012) 8 SCC 21, Kamel Singh (1995) 5 SCC 518, Wahid Khan (2010) 2 SCC 9, Chhotey Lal (2011) 2 SCC 550 (cited in arguments/referred to)
